newsitem.title: USA: Clinton asks Congress to free birth control funds.
newsitem.headline: Clinton asks Congress to free birth control funds.

text.p: President Bill Clinton urged Congress on Friday to release $123 million for spending on birth control overseas and immediately drew fire from anti-abortion forces.

To delay spending the money, Clinton said, would deny safe and effective contraception to couples who depend on these programmes and would lead to "a rise in unintended pregnancies and maternal deaths and a tragic recourse to unsafe and unsanitary methods to terminate those pregnancies."
Congress last year voted to reduce money for international family planning programmes by 35 percent and prevent any further spending until July 1.
But it agreed that if the Clinton government could prove family programmes were being hurt, it would reconsider the measure in February and allow earlier release of the money.

"At issue is whether the money will be released on March 1, or whether it will be further delayed by four months, until July," Clinton said in a written statement. "It is my determination that a delay will cause serious, irreversible and avoidable harm."

Congress last year appropriated $385 million for the State Department's Agency for International Development, but set up a system to allow only part of it to be spent each month. If the money starts flowing in March, the family planning programmes globally would receive $215 million between then and the end of the fiscal year, Sept. 30.
If delayed until July, the programmes would only get $92 million. This means they would get $123 million less than if the money began to be released in March.

Trying to head off criticism, Clinton said opponents have tried to mischaracterize the upcoming congressional vote as one for or against abortion. In fact, he said, the programmes have prevented "untold numbers" of abortions.
"So, let me be clear: the United States provides family planning support where it is wanted and needed. We are prohibited by law from ever funding abortion -- and we abide faithfully by that law."

But the National Conference of Catholic Bishops said the programmes amount to "exporting abortions to developing nations" because the money goes to organisations that perform and promote abortion in these nations.

"Congress will have an opportunity in February to expose this ploy by defeating the administration's proposal and insisting that integrity be restored to the foreign aid programme," said Cardinal Bernard Law, chairman of the U.S. Catholic bishops' Committee for Pro-Life Activities.
